comment:
Dear Administrator Regan and Assistant Administrator Fox,

The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements released by the Environmental Protection Agency in docket EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 take critical steps towards minimizing the presence of lead in drinking water across the country. However, there is no safe level of lead in drinking water, and I urge the EPA to further strengthen and expedite regulations that would protect the tens of millions of Americans who receive their drinking water from lead service lines.

Achieving 100% lead service line replacement within 10 years is a strong action that should be implemented across the country. Cities like Chicago should be held to the same standard; nearly 400,000 lead service lines run through the city, heavily impacting low-income households and communities of color, and an analysis of residential water testing conducted between 2016-2021 found that one in 20 households tested exceeded the federal action levels for lead. Strong action must be taken to expedite the process to remove lead service lines in severely impacted communities.

The practice of splitting funding for lead service line replacement between utilities and water service customers places a financial burden on the communities that have already suffered the disproportionate impacts of lead service lines, from health complications to the costs of alternative water sources. I urge the EPA to follow the example of Michigan’s Lead and Copper Rule, and require public water utilities to cover the full costs of lead service replacement.

In addition to lead service line replacement, there are additional protective steps that the EPA should incorporate into the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements to minimize exposure to and effects of lead contamination. A filter first policy is a key line of defense against lead poisoning, especially in schools and child care centers, and the EPA should match state policies such as Michigan’s and require the installation of filtered drinking water stations or filtered faucets designated for drinking water at those facilities.

Finally, I applaud the progress of lowering the federal action limit from 15 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion. However, that adjustment alone will be insufficient in protecting people from the health impacts of lead exposure, and falls short of the standards set in Canada and recommendations by the EU for triggering action at 5 parts per billion.

Please protect our communities from the hazards of lead contamination and take equitable and immediate action to get the lead out of our drinking water.

Respectfully,

Caleb Merendino

comment:
El Paso Water’s top priority is to ensure safe, reliable water for our customers. We support EPA’s objectives to better protect communities from risks of lead exposure by removing lead from our nation’s drinking water; however, we request adequate flexibility and resource support and urge EPA to consider community needs before finalizing the Lead and Copper Improvements (LCRI).

As background, while lead is not a concern in our source water supply or with water from our treatment plants or water mains, it may be present in older service lines, connectors or within customers’ indoor plumbing fixtures.

Lead connectors: EPA requests comment on whether the Agency should include lead connectors as part of mandatory replacement. EPWater agrees with EPA’s approach to not include lead connectors for replacement. Even by adding the connectors to the inventory as part of LCRI creates an additional regulatory framework on top of the existing requirements under the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) for populating an inventory of lead connectors. While these were not included in the LCRR, the LCRI requires these lead connectors be added to the LCRR inventory no later than October 16, 2024. Records on lead connectors can be limited at best, and this requirement is burdensome with little public health benefit. Additionally, an inventory of lead connectors will most always require excavation, and this combined with the tight deadline may not be feasible or practical for us or many municipal utilities. We request that the timeline for completion of LCRR inventory be extended to allow utilities to fully compile a reliable inventory.

Tap sampling results in three days: EPA is proposing that water systems provide consumer notices of individual tap sampling results within three calendar days of obtaining them, regardless of whether those results exceeded the action level or not. We do not think this is feasible as written. We are particularly concerned about sampling that may occur on a Thursday or Friday or in the cases when there is a holiday weekend. We would strongly recommend that, at a minimum this be changed to reflect three business days, but five business days would be far more preferable and realistic.

Private side of the service lines: Any final LCRI rulemaking should clarify the replacement requirements of customer-owned portions of lead service lines. Currently the proposed rule is unclear and may unintentionally place that burden on municipal utilities like El Paso Water. Moreover, since excavation is likely required, there are questions on liability for damaged property, including damage to other utilities like cable, gas, or electric.

The LCRI also seems to equate access to private property with control of the private side of the service line. The water utility is generally unable to access the customer-owned portion of the service line without the customer’s permission. Nor is the utility under any obligation to replace or pay for replacement of the customer portion of a service line that fails since it is the customer’s private property. If a customer does not grant permission to property, and the homeowner cannot afford to replace the line, there should be clearer guidance of expectations.

Private plumbing system accommodations: With the possibility of lead being introduced through private premise plumbing systems, it is important that any trigger levels allow for this possibility. El Paso Water is confident that our source water, treatment facilities, and water mains do not introduce lead into the drinking water supply, but we are concerned with the possibility that customers’ private plumbing systems could introduce lead detectable at the tap and trigger regulatory action. We ask EPA to consider this scenario in its final recommendations.

Funding for private service lines, especially in disadvantaged communities: the Administration in its annual budget should also request from Congress the necessary funding to help with service line replacement for those customers who cannot afford it on their own. Any funds provided for drinking water improvements should be prioritized for disadvantaged communities. El Paso is a community with large numbers of low-income households and other marginalized populations. These underserved areas often face severe economic hardships. Without adequate funding from the federal government, they would have little to no ability to pay for replacement of lead service lines.

Municipal utilities are not-for-profit public entities, and this proposed rule may misplace enormous financial and legal obligations upon them thereby undercutting the public health benefits the rule intends to provide. The EPA should consider refining changes to the LCRI to address responsibility and liability concerns for the replacement of customer-owned lead service lines to remove potential costs burdens from municipal utilities and their customers.

comment:
I own two rental houses in Lansing, Michigan. Although I have replaced all of the pipes inside the houses with copper, using lead free solder, the service lines are lead and I can do nothing about that. I have put filters on the sinks but tenants always remove them as they are inconvenient, ugly, and a maintenance hassle. The only way to prevent lead in my tenant's drinking water is for the utility (Lansing Board of Water and Light) to replace the service lines.

Thank you for proposing stronger regulations to protect people from lead in drinking water. We know that drinking water contamination disproportionately affects low wealth families such as my tenants. And we know that ending the nationwide crisis of lead in water is a priority for this administration.

That is why requiring removal of all lead service lines in most water systems in ten years is a massive step towards ensuring nobody is living with exposure to lead. Improving sampling requirements and lowering the EPA’s lead action level are also extremely important changes that will help communities across the nation.

However, we need EPA to ensure the final rule is even stronger or else the goals of the administration will not be met and future generations of children will be exposed to lead from drinking water. Some crucial improvements would be:
-Remove the exceptions to the 10- year lead pipe removal mandate that allow some systems to stretch that deadline
- Close loopholes allowing water systems to remove some lead service lines from the replacement pool (and therefore not replace all of them)
-Mandate that water utilities fully pay for the removal of lead service lines and replace them with lines made from sustainably-sourced copper. This is a public health issue that disproportionately affects communities of color and low-wealth communities. Removal can cost thousands of dollars: we must ensure that removal does not occur only for the wealthy. Landlords such as myself could only pay for such improvements through passing on the cost to our tenants via increased rent. Pricing poor families out of their housing in the name of pure water is not a viable solution.
-Incentivize older schools to install filters to ensure that children who spend many hours there daily are not at high risk of exposure.

Not addressing these components would allow for environmental injustice to persist. It is unjust and unfair to ask people who did not choose the zip code they were born in to bear decades more of exposure because they cannot afford to fix the contaminated lead service lines.

We urge you to quickly finalize a strong and equitable rule, so that all communities can see a significant decrease in lead in their drinking water. This would be a legacy defining achievement by this administration and would be an incredible boon for communities across the country. Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Christopher Rathbun
East Lansing, MI

As a retired school psychologist and educational administrator, I know that there is no safe level of lead for a child's development. Lead exposure causes behavioral disabilities, intellectual disabilities and other learning problems, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and speech delays (https://www.luc.edu/healthyhomes/leadsafeillinois/leadfacts/rippleeffectsofchildhoodleadpoisoning/). The associated economic costs are extraordinary -- well into the billions (https://www.luc.edu/media/lucedu/hhhci/pdf/FactSheetSavingstocommunity.pdf). An estimated 500,000 children in the United States have excessive blood levels of lead (https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/lead/overview.html). And yet, millions of mothers, infants, and children drink tap water served by lead pipes. This is a national crisis that must be addressed without further delay. I urge you to finalize the strongest lead and copper rule possible to attack this public health crisis so everyone can access safer drinking water.

The EPA recently announced a proposal to help get lead out of drinking water, which is a critical step toward addressing this urgent health issue – but the regulations would take a decade to be put into place and allow some utilities to skirt their duty to pay to replace these lead pipes. We need the EPA to finalize strong regulations that:

- Require water utilities to cover the full cost of lead service line replacement, so we’re not putting that financial burden on low-income homeowners, and to protect renters whose landlords are unlikely to pay the cost of lead pipe replacement. This is especially important in environmental justice communities that are already saddled with disproportionate lead contamination.

We don’t want another generation of our kids to be harmed by lead pipes that are contaminating their tap water, or to expose adults with cardiovascular disease to additional long-term risks of a heart attack or even death from prolonged exposure to lead pipes.

Again, developing young brains simply cannot afford to wait years for this problem to be fixed. Our society cannot afford to wait either. Please finalize this rule without delay.

Thank you.

comment:
Lead-Free Water for All - A Time for Action

Issue: Millions of Americans lack access to safe drinking water due to lead contamination, primarily from lead service lines. The EPA's current proposal, while a step forward, doesn't go far enough.

Urgency: Lead is a potent neurotoxin with devastating health consequences, especially for children. Protecting public health demands immediate and comprehensive action.

Demands:

* Full Lead Service Line Replacement: We call for the complete replacement of all lead service lines nationwide within 10 years, at no cost to individual households. No exceptions.
* Ban on Toxic Alternatives: Replacing lead with another harmful material like PVC is unacceptable. The EPA must ban the use of PVC and chlorinated PVC in service lines.
* Stricter Lead Action Level: Lower the action level for lead in drinking water to no more than 5 ppb, reflecting the latest scientific understanding of lead's dangers.
* Protect Public Spaces: Ensure safe water in all public places through mandatory filter-first policies and stringent testing requirements.
* Just and Safe Removal: Prioritize environmental justice by guaranteeing safe and responsible removal and disposal of lead service lines. Oppose the export of lead-contaminated materials to countries with weaker environmental standards.

Why it Matters: Access to safe water is a fundamental human right. This is not merely an environmental issue, but a matter of public health and social justice. Every community and every person deserves lead-free water.

Call to Action: We urge the EPA to adopt these vital measures and work with communities to deliver on the promise of safe drinking water for all. No one should be left behind in this critical effort to protect our health and well-being. By taking a bold and comprehensive approach, we can safeguard public health, ensure environmental justice, and build a future where every person has access to safe, clean water.

This statement can be used to engage with policymakers, businesses, communities, and the public to build support for a strengthened EPA regulation and accelerate the nationwide effort to eliminate lead from our drinking water systems.

I appear before you today to address a critical issue that demands our immediate attention and collective commitment: environmental justice. Throughout history, federal agencies have unfortunately been entangled in discriminatory practices that disproportionately impact marginalized communities. One glaring instance of such historical injustice is exemplified by the lead piping issues in Flint and Benton Harbor, Michigan, underscoring the severe consequences of systemic neglect and environmental injustice.

In these communities, the distribution of resources, particularly in terms of access to clean and safe drinking water, has been marred by discriminatory policies. The lead contamination crisis, notably in Flint, exposed a failure in the provision of a basic human necessity—safe water. The repercussions of this crisis extend beyond immediate health concerns, leaving indelible scars on the affected communities and amplifying existing systemic disadvantages.

The lead piping issues in Flint and Benton Harbor serve as contemporary examples of how federal agencies can perpetuate disparities among racial, ethnic, and low-income communities. The inadequate response to the water crisis exacerbated the challenges faced by these communities, compounding their historical struggles and contributing to a sense of environmental injustice.

It is imperative that we recognize the interconnectedness of historical discrimination and contemporary environmental issues. The lead piping problems in Michigan highlight the need for a comprehensive and equitable approach to environmental policies. These communities deserve more than just acknowledgment of their struggles; they deserve proactive measures to rectify the injustices they have endured.

It is also imperative that we do not allow such discriminatory practices to persist or, worse, exacerbate the already existing issues of environmental injustice. Environmental justice, at its core, demands that every individual, regardless of their background, has the right to a clean and safe environment. It necessitates a paradigm shift in how we approach policy-making, ensuring that the burdens and benefits of environmental policies are distributed equitably.

To achieve this, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) must play a pivotal role. The EPA must not only acknowledge historical injustices but also actively work to rectify them. Mere assessments and identifications of disparate impacts are not sufficient; there must be a meaningful commitment to listening to the voices of environmental justice community advocates. The EPA must actively engage with and incorporate the insights, concerns, and recommendations of these advocates into their decision-making processes.

Preventing disparate impacts is not just a regulatory requirement; it is a moral imperative. The EPA must adopt policies and practices that prioritize the well-being of environmental justice communities, ensuring that they are not disproportionately burdened by environmental hazards or deprived of the benefits of a healthy environment.

The regulations set by the EPA aimed to protect public health by establishing standards for the allowable levels of lead and copper in drinking water. The Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) is a specific regulation under the NPDWR that addresses these contaminants.

Improvements to the regulations may include updates to standards, testing requirements, monitoring procedures, and public notification protocols. Improvements are often driven by advances in scientific understanding, technological developments, and experiences gained from incidents of water contamination.

Possible areas of improvement could include:

Lowering Action Levels: The EPA might consider lowering the action levels for lead and copper in drinking water to reflect updated health risk assessments.
Enhanced Monitoring: Improved methods of monitoring and testing for lead and copper could be implemented to ensure more accurate and timely identification of water quality issues.
Public Education and Notification: Strengthening requirements for public education and notification about lead and copper levels in drinking water can help raise awareness and empower communities to take action.
Lead Service Line Replacement: Regulations might be updated to accelerate the replacement of lead service lines, which are a significant source of lead contamination in drinking water.
Infrastructure Investment: Increased emphasis on funding and support for water infrastructure projects to address aging pipes and mitigate the risk of lead and copper leaching into the water supply.
Compliance and Enforcement: Strengthening measures for ensuring water systems' compliance with regulations and enhancing enforcement mechanisms to hold non-compliant entities accountable.

No lead is safe, and the new proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements will significantly benefit lead poisoning prevention efforts and its countless social, health, and economic benefits.

comment:
The International Society for Environmental Epidemiology (ISEE) is a multidisciplinary, scientific society dedicated to the study of environmental epidemiology and exposure assessment; our membership is drawn from more than 60 countries. Our primary objective is promoting research and disseminating scientific findings focused on the relationships between environmental exposures (e.g., air pollutants, food and water contaminants, metals, etc.) and human health. We are oriented particularly toward improving the science that governments use to guide environmental health policy.

ISEE-North America represents environmental researchers at universities, health and policy organizations, governmental agencies, industrial associations, and public interest organizations from throughout North America. We have comments addressing both overarching issues, as well as specific comments tied to the particulars of EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Thank you for soliciting input on it.

We have strongly supported EPA’s holistic approach in its Lead Strategy. The LCRI could be a strong tool in EPA’s arsenal, but serious omissions undermine its effectiveness.

There are many improvements in the LCRI. We commend EPA for
increasing the regulated universe of lead pipes for replacement to 9 million.
reducing the time frame of the regulation to 10 years.
lowering the Action Level (AL) to from 15 to 10 ppb.
taking both a first- and fifth-liter sample, with the higher level to constitute compliance.
requiring water systems to deliver the results of home testing to the residents within 3 days of sampling, regardless of the levels in the sample.
proposing “whenever there is a change in ownership, even after the mandatory service line replacement deadline has passed, the system would be required to offer to conduct the replacement.”

KEY COMMENTS

We have 11 principal recommendations. Detailed discussions follow.

1.Multiple studies show that within the general population and across numerous health endpoints, water lead levels (WLLs) at current compliance levels have clinical significance. The AL should be reduced to 5 ppb.
2.Omitting schools and other child-occupied buildings from this regulation leaves the most vulnerable part of the population susceptible to uncontrolled lead exposures. The most efficient way to address this is by requiring water systems to install and maintain water filters on all faucets that may be used for drinking within such buildings.
3.Partial pipe replacement should not be permitted. Partial replacements are more likely to occur in low income and disadvantaged communities.
4.EPA should pressure PWSs to replace the entire LSL.
5.EPA should encourage states to give public water systems the authority to use ratepayer funds to replace LSLs and GRRs on private property.
6.To reduce the complexity of the LCRI, a single exceedance of the AL should constitute a violation with resulting public education, point-of-use (POU) requirements, etc.
7.Mandatory POU filters should follow all exceedances.
8.The paucity of monetized benefits, especially health benefits, and the heavy documentation of costs shows evidence of systemic bias.
9.We recommend better tracking of public water system (PWS) water monitoring and reporting results by the State primacy agency, which may include a primacy requirement related to the completeness and accuracy of reporting.
10.EPA must report the full range of materials and health benefits using a 2% discount rate.
11.EPA should prohibit ‘gaming’ both explicitly and generally, including deleting outliers.

comment:
1. Clarification needed on §141.81(a)(1) and (2) are for large and medium "community" water systems and does not include non-transient, non-community water systems.
2. Provision under §141.81(f) can be a loophole for large community water system without CCT to get away from treatment technique requirement if the system intentionally list some galvanized pipe as GRR (ie. stating that they have unknown line with galvanized pipe downstream) in its inventory when it expects to exceed the PQL for lead. Without GRR, system would have been required to install CCT.
3. Provision under §141.84(d)(3)(ii) where requiring PWS to offer full service line replacement to any new property owner within 6 months of any change in ownership of property is hard to implement. First, PWS does not have access to deed. Second, even if PWS has access to deed, it's hard for PWS to know if there is a true change in ownership (ie. a house may be owned by a single person. That person gets married and add his/her spouse to deed. While the ownership seem to changed according to deed, the actual person living in the property remains the same). Need clarification on the definition of "change in ownership". In addition, the last sentence where it states "this paragraph continues to apply after a system completes its mandatory service line replacement program" doesn't make sense. If everything is done, why further replacement is required?
4. Under §141.85(c), system that exceed lead action level or system with lead, GRR, or lead status unknown service line must offer to sample for lead in the tap water of any customer who requests it. What if the system successfully replaces lead, GRR, or lead status unknown service line prior to offering the sampling? May system obtain waiver for this paragraph?
5. Under §141.85(e)(2), PWS should provide notice to new customer if PWS still has lead, GRR, or unknown service line at the time of service initiation. How can a primacy agency tracks this task? Need a guidance on this.
6. Under §141.86(b)(ii), it states that " to collect a first liter and fifth liter paired sample, systems must collect tap water in five consecutively numbered, wide-mouth, one-liter sample bottles after the water has stood motionless in the plumbing of each sampling site, including the service line, for at least six hours without flushing the tap prior to sample collection." The issue here is the statement "including the service line". In some cases, it is impossible to ensure the service line has stagnant water even if no one is using the water. For example, many water systems have dual service line where one lateral splits into two lines to serve multiple homes. In this case, stagnation at service line is impossible and unfeasible. Suggesting EPA to eliminate the term "including the service line".
7. Need clarification on §141.87 whether "all large water systems" include all large community water systems and large non-transient non-community water systems.
8. Under §141.92(g)(1), CWS must provide lead sampling results to schools within 30 days. The timing doesn't make sense when results from compliance samples require 24 hours notice whereas schools that serve sensitive population may need to wait 30 days to obtain the results.

comment:
NETWORK Lobby for Catholic Social Justice: Comments in Support of Notice of Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper Improvements, EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
Founded more than 50 years ago by Catholic Sisters and guided by fundamental Catholic social justice principles, NETWORK Lobby for Catholic Social Justice is deeply committed to advocating for policies that protect vulnerable communities and advance the common good. As Pope Francis has warned repeatedly, the pursuit of social and economic justice is intertwined with the existential challenges of our world’s environmental crisis. As scientists and policymakers have known for decades, drinking water lead contamination presents just such a tragic and ongoing environmental crisis for our nation’s vulnerable communities, especially for its children.
It has been long established that lead exposure causes severe, irreversible cognitive damage and other grave health problems, with its most devastating impacts on small children. Moreover, as both well-documented studies and the real-world experience of vulnerable communities like Flint, Michigan have shown all too clearly, our Black, Brown and rural neighbors, their families, and their children disproportionately bear the burdens of lead-contaminated drinking water.
Accordingly, NETWORK expresses its strong support for the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA), National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper Improvements (LCRI). The LCRI will, at last, require the removal and replacement of leaded service lines across the nation within 10 years. The proposed rule will also enhance requirements for U.S. water systems to: better identify and report the location of lead service lines; sample water supply lead levels; and take action sooner when such sampling detects elevated lead levels to inform affected residents and reduce their toxic exposure.
It is essential that all of these regulatory measures be implemented promptly. According to EPA estimates, there are still more than 9 million lead pipes currently contaminating the nation’s water supplies. But even these alarming estimates may undercount the proliferation of lead service lines, as 32 states acknowledged in 2021 that they do not even track the number of lead pipes in their water systems. By any estimate, however, the extent of lead pipe contamination into our water systems is a public health crisis, and the proposed LCRI rules set a firm and essential goal toward solving that crisis.
Removing lead pipes from the U.S. water supply in 10 years will be costly. The EPA estimates that full achievement of this goal could cost up to $45 billion. Fortunately, the Biden administration’s Infrastructure Bill already provides $15billion for lead pipe removal, and the proposed rule allows cities with the worst lead pipe volumes to obtain extended time for their removal. As the EPA, municipalities, and water systems determine funding mechanisms to meet the new rule, it is most imperative that none of the costs of lead removal fall on Black, Brown, and rural communities and families who have already borne the burdens and harms of lead contamination for decades.
Children as our nation’s future is a common theme in public discourse, but these are merely empty words without environmental justice policies, including the elimination of the scourge of lead contamination, that will give all children the opportunity to grow and thrive. The proposed LCRI regulations are long overdue, and NETWORK Lobby for Catholic Social Justice urges their prompt final adoption and implementation.

comment:
The EPA estimates there are 9.2 million lead service lines in the United States, with other research estimating as many as 12 million lead service lines bringing water to 22 million people. While the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement requires lead service lines be replaced within 10 years, this will leave many families with toxic lead in their water for years during the rules implementation and line replacement, while cities currently eligible for timeline extensions such as Chicago will be without lead-free water for as many as 40 years. World health experts agree there is no safe level of lead. Even low levels of lead exposure can cause children and those still in the womb to develop brain and nervous system damage, learning disabilities, reduced physical growth, and impaired hearing and speech abilities.

The proposed LCRI does require water systems with consistently high levels of lead to make available to customers filters certified to remove lead from water. However, this language must be strengthened with the following measures to ensure expedient access to clean drinking water. EPA must require water systems to fund the purchase and distribution of filters to customers while also providing education materials and training on filter efficacy and maintenance. Proper distribution and education is critical to ensuring customers can access, trust, and properly use their filter, as seen in Denver, Colorado where, with advanced distribution and education measures, the city achieved 80% filter adoption rates. The EPA must also minimize the period families must wait for a filter by reducing the time and number of lead level exceedances required to constitute “consistently high levels of lead” and expedite filter program implementation. A “filter first” approach will ensure families have access to clean, safe drinking water in the many years to come as the LCRI is implemented and lead service lines are replaced.

comment:
I cannot believe we’re still talking about the elimination of lead in our water supplies after many, many decades of knowing about its toxicity and its impact to our children. It’s time we put this issue to bed. I would have thought that after the Flint, Michigan fiasco lead contamination in our water supplies would have risen to the top of the EPA’s “Things That Need To Be Resolved Immediately” list. After all, isn’t it your responsibility to keep us safe? Instead, here we are 10 years after the Flint catastrophe and we’re still without any meaningful legislation in place that addresses this issue. With that said, being late to the party is better than not showing up at all. So, after 50+ years of knowing about lead poisoning, thank you for proposing stronger regulations to protect people from lead in drinking water.

We know that drinking water contamination disproportionately affects low wealth families and communities of color. And we know that ending the nationwide crisis of lead in water is a priority for this administration.

That is why requiring removal of all lead service lines in most water systems in ten years is a massive step towards ensuring nobody is living with exposure to lead. Improving sampling requirements and lowering the EPA’s lead action level are also extremely important changes that will help communities across the nation.

However, we need EPA to ensure the final rule is even stronger or else the goals of the administration will not be met and future generations of children will be exposed to lead from drinking water. Some crucial improvements would be:
-Remove the exceptions to the 10- year lead pipe removal mandate that allow some systems to stretch that deadline
- Close loopholes allowing water systems to remove some lead service lines from the replacement pool (and therefore not replace all of them)
-Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines and replace them with lines made from sustainably-sourced copper. This is a public health issue that disproportionately affects communities of color and low-wealth communities. Removal can cost thousands of dollars: we must ensure that removal does not occur only for the wealthy.
-Incentivize schools to install filters to ensure that children who spend many hours there daily are not at high risk of exposure.

Not addressing these components would allow for environmental injustice to persist. It is unjust and unfair to ask people who did not choose the zip code they were born in to bear decades more of exposure because they cannot afford to fix the contaminated lead service lines.

We urge you to quickly finalize a strong and equitable rule, so that all communities can see a significant decrease in lead in their drinking water. This would be a legacy defining achievement by this administration and would be an incredible boon for communities across the country. Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Gary Murdock
Cold Brook, NY

comment:
When reviewing the EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), the following aspects stand out to me:

1. The mandate for 100% lead pipe replacement within 10 years prioritizes preventive measures and significantly reduces potential lead exposure.

2. Requiring regular updates to service line inventories and public availability of replacement plans requires knowledge of legacy lead pipes to ensure efficient and equitable replacements.

3. Improved tap sampling protocols enhance accuracy in assessing lead levels and ensure more precise compliance determinations.

4. The proposal to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L reflects a commitment to earlier and more decisive action. This change ensures prompt public notification and mitigation efforts, reinforcing overall health protections.

5. Requiring additional outreach and providing certified lead-reducing filters for water systems with multiple lead action level exceedances demonstrates a commitment to addressing persistent issues promptly.

Final thoughts: while it is evident that the EPA seeks to streamline implementation, reduce complexity, and enhance transparency, challenges in implementing these rules arise, especially for smaller water systems. For example, the ways in which we can ensure equitable access to resources for lead service line replacement considering potential disparities across communities proves highly relevant.

comment:
Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements.
Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801

To U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA),

As a nurse I’ve witnessed how Social Determinants of health can influence people’s health and quality of life. Besides economic instability and limited access to healthcare; environmental factors such as lead contaminated water can have an adverse impact on overall health and well-being.
Lead is a non-biodegradable metal that is toxic to body systems. Infants, young children, and pregnant women are vulnerable to the harmful effects of lead. Despite improvements in water treatment standards and The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), lead exposure remains a concern for vulnerable populations. Therefore, it is reasonable to reduce lead Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) from current action Level of 0.015 mg/L to 0.010 mg/L, with the Maximum Contaminant Level Goals (MCLGs) of zero.
Lead found in tap water usually comes from corrosion or decay of older fixtures or from the solder that connects pipes. While individuals can avoid drinking lead contaminated water by using filters or purchasing drinking water from certified sources, these are not always attainable to every household especially in low-income families. Primary prevention in lead exposure is to remove lead hazards from the environment by proposing the required water systems to replace lead service lines.
Since a blood test is the only way to determine exposure to lead. Having blood lead level testing and follow-up care are secondary prevention. Both primary and secondary preventions can be implemented through public education and increase consumer awareness.
In conclusion, lead poisoning is preventable. Everyone drinks water and the interventions to ensure safe drinking water for everyone should be feasible. Lead MCL should be as close to zero as possible. Special funds should be given for total lead service line replacements, especially for disadvantaged communities.

comment:
Dear Administrator Regan:

We write today as elected officials representing constituents in Chicago, IL to submit public comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). We share a common interest in protecting our communities from the adverse health risks associated with contaminated drinking water. Chicago has approximately 409,000 lead service lines, more than any other city in the country, and we seek your partnership as we build on our progress to expedite the replacement process.

We applaud the EPA’s leadership in unveiling the LCRI proposal and its commitment to fully replacing the nation’s lead pipes within 10 years. As you know, low-income communities and communities of color are disproportionately impacted by contaminated drinking water. Even the lowest level of lead exposure can cause emotional and behavioral issues in children and cardiovascular and maternal health issues in adults – sometimes fatal. The presence of lead pipes is a public health threat and an environmental justice issue, and it’s imperative that our most impacted communities are prioritized throughout the replacement process.

While there’s a lot to praise in the LCRI proposal, there are a few key components that we urge the agency to address in order to strengthen the rule:

Reconsider the exception to the 10-year removal mandate: Chicago would receive an extension of 44.6 to 55.8 years to replace our lead service lines. It is unconscionable to tell Chicago residents that they have to wait generations for safe drinking water. Although we appreciate the flexibility we have been offered, we would like to discuss a shortened timeline that’s coupled with adequate federal funding to complement our efforts.

Require water systems to fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: It can cost $30,000 or more for a resident to replace a single lead service line in Chicago. Although the Chicago Department of Water Management is exploring ways to reduce the cost of replacement and currently offers various programs to incentivize homeowners to take on replacement, we’ve seen in other cities that it’s less expensive, faster, and more equitable to have the utility cover the full cost of lead service line replacement. A resident should not be denied access to safe drinking water because of their lack of ability to pay or landlord absenteeism.

Enact strong protections for schools and childcare centers of all sizes, including filter installation: While some smaller schools and childcare centers that are serviced by a lead service line and/or lead fixtures may benefit from the proposed rule, larger schools and childcare centers will be left out because the proposal’s testing program retains weak elements from the previous rule. We urge the EPA to require comprehensive lead testing in all schools and childcare centers and point-of-use filters to protect the health and safety of our children, regardless of where they’re enrolled.

Reduce lead action level to 5 ppb: We applaud the agency’s step in reducing the lead action level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb, but it’s important that we take another step and lower the action level to 5 ppb to be on par with the drinking water standards of other countries, such as Canada and the European Union, as well as recommendations from the medical and public health community.

Although there is room for improvement in the LCRI proposal, we commend the EPA’s commitment to improving drinking water protections across the nation. Chicago has benefited from this commitment as a recipient of a $336M WIFIA loan to support our lead service line replacement efforts. As elected officials representing a renter-dominated city, we hope you consider our recommendations for the best way to achieve success, as we’ve seen in cities like Newark, NJ, and ensure that our most impacted communities are prioritized.

Thank you Administrator Regan, Assistant Administrator Fox, and all EPA members involved for your continued support and leadership.

Sincerely,

Chairperson Gilbert Villegas, Committee on Economic, Capital and Technology Development
Chairperson Maria Hadden, Committee on Environmental Protection and Energy

I am a US citizen and a Chicago resident. I am a wife, a mother,and a retired clinical social worker with over four decades of experience in healthcare. I fear our children and all life forms on Earth are facing an unhealthy future due to humanity's devastating impact on the planet through toxic pollution and a disregard for nature and its wildlife. It is essential for us to recognize our role as stewards and work diligently to preserve all living beings and ecosystems. Part of this vitally important work is rapidly replacing toxic lead pipes all across the United States.

Thank you for your recently announced proposal to replace 100% of lead pipes for the vast majority of water systems by 2037 and strictly limit partial replacements. Recognizing that there is no safe level of exposure to lead, EPA must adopt strong standards that help our nation address one of the biggest environmental injustices of our time—exposure to toxic lead pipes. Please continue to engage with communities and adopt strong standards that address lead pipes in the most transparent, equitable, and expedited way possible. I encourage you to act with urgency to protect public health by finalizing the most ambitious rule possible by October 2024.

comment:
Thank you for proposing stronger regulations to protect people from lead in drinking water. Our small community of 601 residents were subjected to a contaminated oil well's brine disposal in July of 2023.. It has been a terrible ordeal, with the well 's operator still not making the remedial work detailed in a court order by the EPA. We know that drinking water contamination is especially dangerous in low income areas such as Venango Co, PA, where we live. Houses are old, mine was built by my Great Grandfather in 1916. He used the common plumbing material of that era which was lead. We who have aging homes to keep up are struggling to maintain old equipment which is almost cost prohibitive in our low-income economy.

That is why requiring removal of all lead service lines in most water systems in ten years is a massive step towards ensuring nobody is living with exposure to lead. Improving sampling requirements and lowering the EPA’s lead action level are also extremely important changes that will help communities across the nation.

However, we need EPA to ensure the final rule is even stronger or else the goals of the administration will not be met and future generations of children will be exposed to lead from drinking water. Some crucial improvements would be:
-Remove the exceptions to the 10- year lead pipe removal mandate that allow some systems to stretch that deadline
- Close loopholes allowing water systems to remove some lead service lines from the replacement pool (and therefore not replace all of them)
-Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines and replace them with lines made from sustainably-sourced copper. This is a public health issue that disproportionately affects communities of color and low-wealth communities. Removal can cost thousands of dollars: we must ensure that removal does not occur only for the wealthy.
-Incentivize schools to install filters to ensure that children who spend many hours there daily are not at high risk of exposure.

Not addressing these components would allow for environmental injustice to persist. It is unjust and unfair to ask people who did not choose the zip code they were born in to bear decades more of exposure because they cannot afford to fix the contaminated lead service lines.

The EPA has effectively been neutralized by recent legislation to cut finances and decrease staffing. Our local EPA in Western PA relies on operators to "self-report" when there is a spill, dump, or other accidental contamination of a water source. How likely is that? Of course it isn't reported until someone gets sick or farm livestock start to die. And now we know that even when it is reported by the supplier of the community water to the EPA, they are unable or unwilling to enforce their own court orders.

We urge you to quickly finalize a strong and equitable rule, so that all communities can see a significant decrease in lead in their drinking water. This would be a legacy defining achievement by this administration and would be an incredible boon for communities across the country. Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Maryjane Allen
Reno, PA

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency,

RE: Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements

Dear Sir or Madame:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The Washington Association of Sewer and Water Districts (WASWD) represents more than 180 public water and sewer districts throughout the state, serving nearly 20% of our state’s population. WASWD members provide these cost-effective essential public services in the state’s largest population centers and in the smallest rural communities. Safe drinking water is a major concern to both our membership and the customers they serve. We support strong protections for drinking water from the source to the tap that are furthered with the LCRI. We do have some concerns, however, with the proposed LCRI.

Frequency of lead service line (LSL) inventories: Annual updates are impractical as they are required too frequently. Particularly in areas of the country where lead service lines were infrequently utilized, conducting LSL inventories at this frequency would take up valuable time and resources that could be used for other public health issues such as PFAS. For smaller utilities with few staff the frequency of the inventories is especially a real burden. A longer time frame for updating inventories is warranted for these reasons.

Timeframe for compliance: Optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT) is working well in many jurisdictions where LSLs are present. These systems should have extended time frames for replacement of LSLs since they have already taken action and made capital investments to control lead and copper in their water systems. Health and safety is not at issue in these systems as it is in those with no OCCT, so allowing them to spread out the time and money needed to replace LSLs makes economic sense.

Private service line obligations: In Exhibit 1 on page 84886 of the Register, it summarizes:
“Systems conducting partial service line replacement must offer to replace the remaining portion of the service line not under their control (within 45 days in emergencies)”
In some states, such as Washington, this is not legal. Public funds cannot be spent on private property. Public utilities are able to do work on private property and charge costs to the owner. For example, some utilities have done initial line installation and extended repayment over a number of years via utility billing. However, state law does not allow the utility to force the owner to replace the line, or even to enter onto the property without the owner’s consent unless it is recorded on the original site plans, which it would not be with older development that is most likely to have LSLs. This poses a significant obstacle to compliance with this provision.

Education Requirements: Required public education and its timing need to be simplified and scalable for different sizes of utilities. These programs should be developed by a central agency, such as a state health authority, who is aware of the needs of local utilities. It is too much to expect small utilities to do this on their own when they have few staff.

Funding: Funding for inventories and replacements will always be an issue. The financial pressures for meeting these requirements at the same time as working to meet other regulatory requirements are high, particularly on smaller utilities. Without ongoing federal funding, customers will experience rising utility rates that will be unaffordable to some, and potentially jeopardizing secure housing in some communities.
We appreciate the efforts of EPA in ensuring safe drinking water for all Americans.

Sincerely,


Judi Gladstone
Executive Director
WASWD

comment:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). I would like to echo the sentiment of Shellie Chard at the Oklahoma DEQ in that setting standards does not improve health outcomes, it is the implementation of those standards that will lead to improvements. While I do support the call to remove all lead service lines (LSL), I believe water systems are being set up to fail under an unfair burden.

The realities of working at a water system are often overlooked when writing regulations. Today’s water systems are having difficulty finding employees, adapting to climate change, dealing with supply chain issues and the ever increasing financial restrictions that leave a lot of systems without proper funding. While the EPA and primacy agencies are developing regulations and providing guidance, the water systems are solely responsible for implementation. I believe these regulations can be carried out in a manner that shares the responsibility between stakeholders. Alternatives can include:
•The process used by the United States Postal Service to send out COVID-19 tests nationwide can also be setup for supplying filters. Citizens should be able assess their own risk exposure and decide whether or not to request a lead filter. This way, the filter is on hand, and the water system can then use door hangers to let the resident know if/when they need to use the filter.
•Primacy agencies already have voluntary school testing programs in place through The Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act. Instead of relying on water systems to build school testing programs, primacy agencies should continue and expand their programs to meet the 5 year testing requirement. We do not want to invalidate or duplicate the work that is already in progress.
•Private service line inspections and/or LSL replacements can be required as a part of real estate transactions.
•Landlords who refuse to replace their LSL/GRR plumbing lines should be responsible for providing filters to their residents.

Please count the identification of unknown service lines as work towards replacement goals. Some systems have many unknowns but few LSLs. While unknowns service lines count towards setting replacement goals, identifying an unknown as non-lead does not count toward meeting that goal. A scenario could happen where a system’s replacement rate would be much higher than the actual number of available LSLs leaving the system in noncompliance.

The use of Predictive/Statistical Modeling can be an integral tool for helping large systems identify their unknown services. For older, larger systems there is often a significant amount of lost documentation leading to a high number of unknowns services, not to mention most systems have no records on private plumbing lines. Predictive/Statistical Modeling could provide a more cost effective approach to identifying unknown services. However, some primacy agencies are reluctant to accept modeling given a lack of guidance from the EPA. This leaves physical excavation as the only means to classify service lines. The EPA should develop a set of metrics to help primacy agencies review modeling proposals.

If nothing else, please delay all LCRR compliance deadlines the full three years to LCRI finalization in 2027. This way water systems can continue building their inventory and have a much clearer picture of where LSL/GRRs are located and which customers need door hangars and filters. If all LCRR requirements are set for October 2024, then a lot of money and effort will be wasted supplying these materials to customers who do not need it. As of today, water systems should be focused on building the best possible inventories in order to use funding in the most efficient way.

I hope the EPA considers these comments in light of additional regulations being finalized for PFAS. The pursuit of removing lead service lines is a just and overdue problem but the LCRI as written will have ripple effects on water systems across the whole country. We appreciate the efforts of the EPA in ensuring safe drinking water for all Americans and incorporating these comments will ensure success for the LCRI.

comment:
Dear Administrator Regan,

The International Society for Environmental Epidemiology (ISEE) is a multidisciplinary, scientific society dedicated to the study of environmental epidemiology and exposure assessment; our membership is drawn from more than 60 countries. Our primary objective is promoting research and disseminating scientific findings focused on the relationships between environmental exposures (e.g., air pollutants, food and water contaminants, metals, etc.) and human health. We are oriented particularly toward improving the science that governments use to guide environmental health policy.

ISEE-North America represents environmental researchers at universities, health and policy organizations, governmental agencies, industrial associations, and public interest organizations from throughout North America. We have comments addressing both overarching issues, as well as specific comments tied to the particulars of EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Thank you for soliciting input on it.

We have strongly supported EPA’s holistic approach in its Lead Strategy. The LCRI could be a strong tool in EPA’s arsenal, but serious omissions undermine its effectiveness.

There are many improvements in the LCRI. We commend EPA for
increasing the regulated universe of lead pipes for replacement to 9 million.
reducing the time frame of the regulation to 10 years.
lowering the Action Level (AL) to from 15 to 10 ppb.
taking both a first- and fifth-liter sample, with the higher level to constitute compliance.
requiring water systems to deliver the results of home testing to the residents within 3 days of sampling, regardless of the levels in the sample.
proposing “whenever there is a change in ownership, even after the mandatory service line replacement deadline has passed, the system would be required to offer to conduct the replacement.”

KEY COMMENTS

We have 11 principal recommendations. Detailed discussions follow.

1.Multiple studies show that within the general population and across numerous health endpoints, water lead levels (WLLs) at current compliance levels have clinical significance. The AL should be reduced to 5 ppb.
2.Omitting schools and other child-occupied buildings from this regulation leaves the most vulnerable part of the population susceptible to uncontrolled lead exposures. The most efficient way to address this is by requiring water systems to install and maintain water filters on all faucets that may be used for drinking within such buildings.
3.Partial pipe replacement should not be permitted. Partial replacements are more likely to occur in low income and disadvantaged communities.
4.EPA should pressure PWSs to replace the entire LSL.
5.EPA should encourage states to give public water systems the authority to use ratepayer funds to replace LSLs and GRRs on private property.
6.To reduce the complexity of the LCRI, a single exceedance of the AL should constitute a violation with resulting public education, point-of-use (POU) requirements, etc.
7.Mandatory POU filters should follow all exceedances.
8.The paucity of monetized benefits, especially health benefits, and the heavy documentation of costs shows evidence of systemic bias.
9.We recommend better tracking of public water system (PWS) water monitoring and reporting results by the State primacy agency, which may include a primacy requirement related to the completeness and accuracy of reporting.
10.EPA must report the full range of materials and health benefits using a 2% discount rate.
11.EPA should prohibit ‘gaming’ both explicitly and generally, including deleting outliers.

comment:
To Whom it May Concern:

I am speaking as director of a small water utility (under 10,000 served) in Ohio.

We employ 3 full-time operators and one part-time operator in addition to me and a part-time customer service representative. Expanding regulations are especially difficult in utilities such as ours who are sometimes hard-pressed just maintaining the water plant and equipment.

Now, about the LCRI:

1.The latest proposal will require all lead lines (public and private) to be replaced within 10 years. That is extremely aggressive. It will put a strain on material and labor resources leading to higher prices, for sure. At today’s prices, this will result in operating budgets at least 50% higher than existing. In view of anticipated inflation as previously noted (and other costs for education and possibly treatment), we could be looking at 100% increase in operating budgets with a rate increase to follow. It will be very problematic to explain to residents we need a 100% rate increase in 3 years. I would like to also point out that in our community, lead lines are starting to fail due to their age. Replacements will be required soon whether there is a regulation or not.

The private line replacement has always been a problem for me. Many people, frankly, can’t afford a new line. And, it is unfair to ask those that either don’t have a lead line, or have recently replaced their lead line, to share in the costs for lead line replacements going forward. That is why I strongly advocate the city assess lead line owners, only. And, we can assist those struggling financially by reducing their portion. However, even if we assess homeowners, I would anticipate many will want to pay their portion over time, effectively making the utility a lending institution (most don’t have 5-10k in funds immediately available). I know the federal government is willing to assist in funding, but currently, our community is only eligible for loan funding help. This provides very limited help and leaves this community in a difficult position. A better approach, in my opinion, would be to make it illegal to sell a house with a private lead water service line. Then, the private lines would be replaced by the owners, as should be the case. LCRI's provision to make 4 attempts to persuade people to replace their line is bothersome for people and burdensome for utilities.

Although unrelated, PFAS regulations are impending as well, which will lead to higher water prices. With lead and PFAS regulations, we could be looking at rates 3 times higher than existing within 5-6 years. We are creating a real affordability crisis.

2.I see the lead action level will be reduced to 10 ug/l from 15 ug/l. In addition, the proposal calls for first and fifth liter sampling. It appears the research shows the fifth liter sampling typically results in a higher lead content. In view of the 10-year lead replacement requirement, this seems to make very little sense. The results could undermine our utility’s message for the last 30 years or so in which we consistently met the EPA’s lead requirement. We stated that our “hard” well water provided protection from lead. If the new testing leads to higher results, how will we explain that to customers? This will cause people to further question public water quality and credibility. Sampling procedures, too, are more complicated. We depend on residents to sample… things are getting more complicated for our volunteer residents and we will have to supply 5 times more bottles than before.

3.I see lots of education requirements, filter requirements, etc. which all will increase burdens on our staff and lead to higher costs and reduced confidence in public water. Is all this necessary if the service lines will be replaced in 10 years? Currently, our community trusts our water safety and quality. We have won a couple of state awards. We have already gotten some pushback from residents while doing the service line inventory work. Many people seem to object to our intrusion - and it will get much worse with this regulation.

4.Finally, I have seen several presentations on “Brain drain” at state and national conferences. There is a concern that retirements will result in less utility knowledge over time unless succession plans are implemented. I think the proposed LCRI will lead to early retirements for many people in upper management (I have talked to a few, although I offer no scientific survey). This will accelerate the “brain drain” timetable (I think prematurely before successors are ready) and likely result in lower water quality going forward in many places. I think that counters the goals we are all pursuing.

I hope you consider my comments as well as other's comments. I read where the last lead regulation revision received 80,000 comments with no subsequent changes. I hope that is not the case herein.

comment:
February 4, 2024
Administrator Dan Regan
Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W.
Mail Code: 1101A
Washington, DC 20460

RE: re EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
Dear Administrator Regan,
I have conducted research on lead in drinking water for almost 40 years. I worked at EPA for almost 38 years, during which I wrote EPA’s initial assessment of the benefits of reducing lead in drinking water (Levin 1986). Indeed, I was the first at EPA to propose that lead be regulated not as a potential contaminant in distribution system water but principally as a corrosion by-product in tap water reaching consumers.
I have comments addressing both overarching issues, as well as specific comments tied to the particulars of EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).
I strongly support EPA’s holistic approach in its Lead Strategy. The LCRI could be a strong tool in EPA’s arsenal, but serious omissions undermine its effectiveness.
There are many improvements in the LCRI. I commend EPA for
increasing the regulated universe of lead pipes for replacement to 9 million.
reducing the time frame of the regulation to 10 years.
lowering the Action Level (AL) to from 15 to 10 ppb.
taking both first- and fifth-liter samples, with the higher level constituting compliance.
requiring water systems to deliver the results of home testing to the residents within 3 days of sampling, regardless of the levels in the sample.
proposing “whenever there is a change in ownership, even after the mandatory service line replacement deadline has passed, the system would be required to offer to conduct the replacement.”
But after 40+ years of observing water system, state and EPA compliance with the LCR, 2 GAO reports and EPA’s own evaluation of the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) compliance, I firmly believe that water systems will continue to inadequately implement the LCR. Reporting of such failures by the primacy agency to EPA occurs just a small fraction of the time. Incomplete implementation, including monitoring and reporting, needs to be better tracked by the primacy agency and EPA as it can mask high lead exposures and poorly protect the public. This constitutes ‘back sliding’. These inadequacies should constitute Health-based Violations of the LCRI.
 
KEY COMMENTS
I have 12 principal recommendations. Detailed discussions follow.
1.Multiple studies show that within the general population and across numerous health endpoints, water lead levels (WLLs) at current compliance levels have clinical significance. The AL should be reduced to 5 ppb.
2.Omitting schools and other child-occupied buildings from this regulation leaves the most vulnerable part of the population susceptible to uncontrolled lead exposures. The most efficient way to address this is by requiring water systems to install and maintain water filters on all faucets that may be used for drinking within such buildings.
3.Partial pipe replacement should not be permitted. Partial replacements are more likely to occur in low income and disadvantaged communities.
4.EPA should pressure PWSs to replace the entire LSL.
5.EPA should encourage states to give public water systems the authority to use ratepayer funds to replace LSLs and GRRs on private property.
6.To reduce the complexity of the LCRI, a single exceedance of the AL should constitute a violation with resulting public education, point-of-use (POU) requirements, etc.
7.Mandatory POU filters should follow all exceedances of the 10 ppb AL.
8.The paucity of monetized benefits, especially health benefits, and the heavy documentation of costs shows evidence of systemic bias.
9.The omission of most anticipated health benefits and incomplete portrayal of those that are included argue that the health benefits should be described as lower bound estimates.
10.EPA must report the full range of materials and health benefits using a 2% discount rate.
11.Water monitoring and reporting results by the public water system (PWS) are poorly tracked by the State primacy agencies. I suggest EPA implements a primacy requirement related to the completeness and accuracy of reporting.
12.EPA should prohibit ‘gaming’ both explicitly and generally, including deleting outliers.

Why did you abandon East Palestine, Ohio? "This is America, and no one is coming’: East Palestine locals say they’re sick from chemical exposure, and no one is helping. COLUMBUS, Ohio – Residents of East Palestine who live near the site of a train derailment say they continue to experience strange illnesses that they believe are connected to the epic release of toxic chemicals along the state’s eastern border.

About one year ago, officials with rail company Norfolk Southern and the state jointly agreed to execute a “controlled burn” of five tank cars within the derailed train that were carrying about 116,000 gallons of vinyl chloride, a hazardous chemical used in the PVC plastics manufacturing process. The burn, the officials said, avoided a possible – and potentially more dangerous – explosion. Since then, residents have said much the same thing in interviews, at a primary clinic opened in town as a response measure, and to researchers: They believe they’ve been exposed to hazardous substances that continue to cause disconcerting symptoms like rashes, nosebleeds and upper respiratory problems. Many voiced struggles in getting state and federal officials to test inside their homes for the presence of toxic substances.
Connecting the sometimes invisible symptoms reported by those exposed to the chemicals to their root cause is difficult. Cleveland.com/The Plain Dealer couldn’t confirm that exposure to the chemicals spilled and burned at the 38-car derailment directly led to the symptoms some residents say they’ve experienced.

While residents report symptoms, the air is safe in the village, according to Norfolk Southern spokesman Bryan Long. He said air monitoring in town is ongoing, “and no detections of any chemical are being found.” Both he and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency have noted that over 115 million air and soil sampling data points and indoor air testing in 600 homes following the initial post-derailment evacuation orders detected no actionable levels of contaminants.“There are patients who have and some who continue to have complaints of chemical exposure,” said Dr. Gretchen Nickell, a physician and medical director at the East Liverpool City Hospital’s East Palestine clinic.

“These symptoms include eyes, nose and throat irritation and complaints. There are some who had and continue to have complaints of shortness of breath and cough and skin rashes.” When will the EPA be setting aside a medical fund for those affected? The future of the residents and their health is unclear. Jessica Conard said in an interview she can still smell chlorine when it rains in town. The tracks run right by her home. She said she still sees rashes pop up on her body. After the derailment, her son was newly diagnosed with asthma, requiring an inhaler twice a day, which she believes is linked to the derailment.

Conard has demands she says are reasonable. Those who lived so close to a derailment and chemical release over which they had no control should be relocated, and supported financially if they can’t afford to do so on their own; they should have the air in their homes monitored for chemical presences; and they should have costs of exposure-related health care covered for life.

Her progress is sparse. Four nearby residents interviewed ahead of the anniversary of the derailment said none of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency, the U.S. EPA, or Norfolk Southern has tested the air in their house. Several said they’re “stuck” in contaminated homes. For almost a year now, Ashley McCollum, her son, her boyfriend, and her pets have bounced from hotel to hotel, living without a kitchen most of the time. But she still must make return trips to her home near the derailment site for the mail, or to check on her house for burst pipes and other problems. “When we go in the house, our lips tingle,” she said. “I have neurological symptoms where my hands twitch, my eyes burn.”

Shortly after the derailment, the company offered to test her home. But she said she didn’t trust the contract they came with, which she said would have allowed multiple different entities on her property, with no fixed end date, bringing trucks and medical detectors and handheld sensors.

“I want them to check my home. Actually check it,” she said. “There’s no way I think I should be feeling the way I do when you’re there.”

Norfolk Southern has paid her thousands in hotel costs since the derailment. But the company has since announced that given the “remediation” phase of the clean-up is over, it will end its relocation assistance program Feb. 9. EPA should step in starting then.

comment:
Dear Mr. Goldberg and the Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water,

The East Chicago Calumet Coalition Community Advisory Group (ECCC-CAG) respectfully submits this Comment on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Lead exposure is a dire health concern to the millions of people who face exposure through legacy industrial pollution, water service lines, soil contamination, workplace hazards, and more. Updating the Lead and Copper Rule is an opportunity to ensure that federal regulations adequately provide for clean, safe drinking water that offers peace of mind and health for Americans nationwide.

Possibly no community has had more exposure to and experience with cumulative lead exposures than East Chicago, Indiana. East Chicago is a low-income, predominantly Black and Brown community that bears the burden of environmental injustice through disproportionate exposure to lead pollution via soil and drinking water contamination. We founded the ECCC-CAG in 2016 to address community needs during the U.S.S. Lead Superfund remediation process, and our group now works to address ongoing environmental issues in our Calumet neighborhood specifically and East Chicago more generally. This comment shares insights gained from East Chicago’s EPA-funded lead service line replacement program that should inform EPA’s development and implementation of the LCRI regulations.

While the ECCC-CAG strongly supports EPA’s efforts to mandate lead service line replacement, lower the lead action level, enhance monitoring of corrosion control treatments, and improve public education, we nonetheless believe these efforts fall short of addressing the full concerns of environmental justice communities. Based on our experiences in East Chicago, the ECCC- CAG urges EPA to strengthen key provisions of the proposed LCRI regulations and (1) require water systems to fund the replacement of privately-owned service lines; (2) further lower the action level to five ug/L; (3) directly participate in monitoring corrosion control treatment; and (4) further expand its public education efforts regarding tenants’ rights and corrosion control. We elaborate further on each of these in the attached comment titled "ECCC-CAG Comment on EPA LCRI."

To U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA),

As a nurse I’ve witnessed how Social Determinants of health can influence people’s health and quality of life. Besides economic instability and limited access to healthcare; environmental factors such as lead contaminated water can have an adverse impact on overall health and well-being.
Lead is a non-biodegradable metal that is toxic to body systems. Infants, young children, and pregnant women are vulnerable to the harmful effects of lead. Despite improvements in water treatment standards and The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), lead exposure remains a concern for vulnerable populations. Therefore, it is reasonable to reduce lead Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) from current action Level of 0.015 mg/L to 0.010 mg/L, with the Maximum Contaminant Level Goals (MCLGs) of zero.
Lead found in tap water usually comes from corrosion or decay of older fixtures or from the solder that connects pipes. While individuals can avoid drinking lead contaminated water by using filters or purchasing drinking water from certified sources, these are not attainable to every household especially in low-income families. Primary prevention in lead exposure is to remove lead hazards from the environment by proposing the required water systems to replace lead service lines.
Since a blood test is the only way to determine exposure to lead. Having blood lead level testing and follow-up care are secondary prevention. Both primary and secondary preventions can be implemented through public education and increase consumer awareness.
In conclusion, lead poisoning is preventable. Everyone drinks water and the interventions to ensure safe drinking water for everyone should be feasible. Lead MCL should be as close to zero as possible. Special funds should be given for total lead service line replacements, especially for disadvantaged communities.
