comment:
The LCRI continues the trend of only considering chemical addition for corrosion control treatment (CCT). This CCT approach relies solely on chemical addition at the entry point to resolve corrosion issues in private premise plumbing systems, which are parts of the water system outside of ownership and direct control of water providers. Unfortunately, this approach ignores the impact that naturally forming biofilms have on water quality variability and corrosion, and incorrectly assumes that chemical addition alone at the entry point, which in some systems is very distant from the end users tap, will dominate scale forming reactions in premise plumbing systems and in lead service lines to negate the presence and actions of biofilm. The reality is that localized biofilm conditions set up in portions of every water system to create low pH hot spots that push against and negate a chemical based CCT approach, creating variability in LCR results. Biofilms performing nitrification are known to create acidity and biofilms that are thick are known to secrete organic acids, both of which will fight against scale formation to negate chemical addition and cause corrosion. Scale-negating biofilm issues become amplified in portions of water systems with high water age, where disinfection is low, including in areas such as dead-end mains, stagnant loops, poorly mixed reservoirs, oversized service lines, oversized plumbing systems and premise plumbing systems with low water usage. This issue has become exacerbated in recent years by a plumbing code that has not kept up with water efficiency practices, requiring plumbing piping sizes that are too large for water demands created by water efficient fixtures, which causes increased stagnancy, biofilm growth, pH fluctuation and microbiologically influenced corrosion in plumbing system. Retrofit of new fixture in older plumbing systems results in a drop in velocity and an increase in stagnancy, which further promotes biofilm growth, debris accumulation and increased MIC issues.

In many cases, optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT) could be achieved with best practices alone, which help maintain disinfection in the water system and help control biofilm, debris accumulation, pH fluctuation and corrosion in premise plumbing systems. Best practices generally include routine unidirectional flushing of water system pipes, scouring of treatment plant intake pipes, chemical rehabilitation of wells, chemical cleaning of treatment plant infrastructure (filter media, membranes, storage, piping, etc), flushing or elimination of dead-end mains, and flushing of service lines at time of meter changeout to bring better water quality and improved disinfection into plumbing systems. In addition, these efforts could be further extended by educating consumers on the importance of keeping their private plumbing systems clean, which would improve public health (reduced nitrification and reduced DBP formation) and improve a water provider’s ability to meet corrosion regulations.

Based on the above, the LCRI should include provisions to allow a water provider the option to demonstrate and implement best management practices for OCCT. This would allow the water provider an opportunity to perform a CCT study that looks at 1) chemical feed alone, 2) a combination of chemical feed and best practices, and/or 3) use of best practices only to achieve OCCT. It also allows the water provider to consider overall costs for the CCT approach, including the need to perform phosphorus removal at the local or regional wastewater treatment facility to meet pollution elimination discharge regulations.

comment:
Please see the attached document for Beyond Plastics' full comment.

The U.S. EPA’s proposal to require water systems to replace lead service lines is excellent news for the health of children and adults nationwide. Lead is a neurotoxin, and there is no safe level of exposure. Unless the EPA provides guidance on suitable replacement materials for lead pipes, however, newly laid infrastructure can easily repeat the harms of the past by swapping out one suite of toxic hazards for another. This is particularly true for plastic piping, such as polyvinyl chloride, which will undoubtedly be considered as a replacement due to its low price point. However, the cost of the replacement pipe is modest compared to the overall cost of the project and should not be a driver in this important decision. PVC and other plastic pipes are petrochemical products made from a mix of chemicals and fossil fuels, many of which are known toxicants with the capacity to leach into drinking water. As with lead, this comes with its own serious health concerns, which should be addressed as part of the LCRI.

After an extensive review of the scientific literature, Beyond Plastics issued a report in April 2023 titled “The Perils of PVC Plastic Pipes.” Based on the findings of this report, Beyond Plastics strongly recommends that the LCRI include detailed guidance on the hazards of PVC and other plastics as replacement water pipes, and consider safer alternatives, such as recycled copper and stainless steel pipes.

Plastic pipes present risk because they release more contaminants into drinking water than unlined metal pipes do. Copper, which has a high thermal rating, is particularly resistant to corrosion and was recently used in New York City and Newark, NJ, to replace lead service lines.

The EPA’s only safety requirement for pipes and other plumbing materials is that they are free of lead. Even so, lead compounds are a common stabilizer used in PVC, so much so that they represent nearly 50% of total stabilizers used in PVC applications. Why would we replace lead pipes with pipes that contain lead?

Time, too, is of the essence. While the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement requires lead service lines be replaced within 10 years, this will leave many families with toxic lead in their water for years during the rules implementation and line replacement, while cities currently eligible for timeline extensions such as Chicago will be without lead-free water for as many as 40 years. The proposed LCRI does require water systems with consistently high levels of lead to make available to customers filters certified to remove lead from water. However, this language must be strengthened with the following measures to ensure expedient access to clean drinking water. EPA must require water systems to fund the purchase and distribution of filters to customers while also providing education materials and training on filter efficacy and maintenance. Proper distribution and education is critical to ensuring customers can access, trust, and properly use their filter, as seen in Denver, Colorado where, with advanced distribution and education measures, the city achieved 80% filter adoption rates. The EPA must also minimize the period families must wait for a filter by reducing the time and number of lead level exceedances required to constitute “consistently high levels of lead” and expedite filter program implementation. A “filter first” approach will ensure families have access to clean, safe drinking water in the many years to come as the LCRI is implemented and lead service lines are replaced.

Communities need to understand the potential health risks associated with different water pipe materials so that they do not select alternatives that turn out to be just as bad, if not worse, as the original option. EPA needs to weigh in on this.

PVC Piping
No matter what they are made of, all pipes can leach their constituent materials to some extent, and the constituent materials of PVC pipes are particularly hazardous to human health. The base material of PVC and CPVC is vinyl chloride, a chemical that has been linked to increased risk of liver, brain, and lung cancers, as well as lymphoma and leukemia, according to the National Institute of Health. The International Agency for Research on Cancer first declared the chemical to be a carcinogen in 1974. In response, the Consumer Product Safety Commission banned its use as an aerosol in consumer products, while the Food and Drug Administration banned its use in cosmetics. The EPA, too, raised serious concerns about the health impacts of vinyl chloride — concerns that assisted the passage of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) 1976. Despite the existing evidence of harm, the EPA fell short of adding vinyl chloride to the list of chemicals governed by the act, though in December 2023, the agency placed it on a short list of high-priority chemicals for reconsideration.

Communities with older housing, lower incomes, and higher rates of minority residents are disproportionately burdened by lead exposure. We need clear, accessible timelines for each community, regular progress updates, and strong enforcement mechanisms to hold both water systems and states accountable for timely replacements.

Many people are unaware of the lead risks lurking in their taps. Educational campaigns can empower individuals to protect themselves and advocate for change. Support community-based efforts. Local organizations and residents often have valuable insights and can play a crucial role in identifying affected areas and mobilizing action.
In conclusion, while I applaud the EPA's steps towards safer drinking water, I urge the agency to accelerate LSL replacement and prioritize high-risk communities. comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

My name is Dr Aisha Harris, MD and I am a family medicine physician at Harris Family Health in Flint, Michigan who provides primary care for diverse and vulnerable populations. Additionally, I participate in health outreach that helps address health and environmental concerns and inequities in the Flint and Genesee County community. Lead exposure during the Flint Water Crisis has negatively impacted our community so I believe in the importance of strong lead regulations that focus on prevention and mitigation via equitable approaches and policies.

I would like to provide feedback on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. In November 2023, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) that provide a critical step to reduce lead in drinking water over the next ten years. I have recommendations that would strengthen these protections to prevent further exposure to lead in environmental justice communities.

Weak lead exposure regulations fail to protect the most vulnerable populations in our community. In Flint, the vulnerable populations include the Black and Brown community, low income households, youth and seniors. Flint is home to approximately 80,000 residents and the median household income is $35,000. There is a large Black and Brown community in Flint, with 56% identifying as African American. Because of sensitive periods of neurodevelopment, it is imperative that kids are protected from the irreversible harms of lead exposure. Here in Flint, 24% of the population is under 18 years and 6.7% of the population is under 5 years. Lead exposure is also particularly harmful for seniors age 65 and up, who make up 13% of the population in Flint. (Census, 2023)

The EPA’s proposal for lead service line replacement is valid but I encourage more robust systems for tracking and stringent regulation of the process across the country. There should be consequences for water systems that do not replace the lead service lines within 10 years. Additionally, it is recommended that lead service line replacement be an opt out procedure in order to be inclusive and equitable in communities where communication is challenging and households residents are not the homeowner. The replacement of lead service lines should be completed and implemented in the most efficient, effective, and equitable way to eliminate exposure to lead and protect public health. There should also be financial prioritization of lead service line replacement in environmental justice communities.

The EPA’s proposal for reducing complexity and improving public health protection was fair, but I encourage this rule to go even further to protect public health. Given that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water, I demand that the federal action level be lowered from 15 ppb, not only to 10 ppb as proposed here, but to 1 ppb to provide the strongest protection possible. I have seen the acute and chronic medical problems that arise from lead exposure in adults and children and believe there is no safe level of lead in drinking water.

Transparency and communication are vital to maintain and build public trust which is essential for safeguarding public health and eliminating health disparities, especially in environmental justice communities. The EPA should have a public notification process that has diverse communication options including digital (website, social media, radio) and in person (flyers, church announcements, etc) to effectively educate and inform communities. Equitable communication strategies would assist residents in lead exposure notification and alert them to when water-related work is occurring in a timely manner. As a primary care doctor, I see the consequences of poor communication and understanding when it comes to mitigation and prevention and know the importance of improving literacy and comprehension to decrease combat public health issues.

Finally, the proposal includes a cost-benefit analysis for making improvements to the Lead and Copper rule. As a resident of Flint and primary care doctor in Flint, I can assure you that there is no dollar amount that could compare to the cost of human life or the irreversible harm caused by lead exposure. In environmental justice communities all across the country, there are people who depend on the government to put forward rules that truly protect our health and well-being no matter the cost.

In closing I appreciate you taking the time to read our comments. Please consider incorporating stricter regulations and stronger protections for drinking water to protect the health of the most vulnerable among us.

Sincerely,
Dr Aisha Harris, MD
Family Medicine Physician
Harris Family Health

comment:
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements
Comments:
We believe the “full replacement” definition in the LCRI to include the property owner’s portion of a service line exceeds the legal authority of any such water system and the legal authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act.
The Safe Drinking Water Act as amended by The Safe Drinking Water Act of 1996 states in Section 1400, Part A, Section 1401
Section 1401. For the purpose of this title:
(1)The term “Primary drinking water regulation” means a regulation which –
(A)Applies to public water systems;
and,
(4) Public Water System
(A)(i) any collection, treatment, storage and distribution facilities under control of the operator of such system and used in primary connection with such system,

In one part of the LCRI, it states that water systems replace service lines and connectors “under control of” that water system. In Texas, that would be the portion of the service line up to the meter. However, later in the LCRI, it states that the EPA has proposed “requirements and flexibilities to increase access and expedite full service line replacement”. This certainly contradicts with the first portion of that proposed rule.
The private, property owners portion of the service line is not owned by the public water system and therefore not “under the control” of the public water system. Therefore, it is not within the legal authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act to regulate this portion of the private connection to the public water system. If a water system is expected to replace the property owner’s portion of the service line, that would require an easement, and the water system now being responsible for that service line, I.e. “taking” ownership of it. In Texas “Taking” is defined in the Property Rights Act section 2007.002(5) as:
(A) a governmental action that affects private real property, in whole or in part or temporarily or permanently, in a manner that requires the governmental entity to compensate the private real property owner as provided by the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution or Section 17 or 19, Article I, Texas Constitution.
Furthermore, the LCRI seems to push water systems to ask for changes to any legislation that would update property rights to meet those set forth in the LCRI. Legislation should not be a bottom-up requirement. Water systems have no authority to propose property rights bills in any State, or especially Federal legislature.
Finally, if property owners are required to replace their portion of the service line, the EPA should provide a funding mechanism for property owners, similar to the CDC’s grant program for individual cities, that came out of the Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Act of 1971, followed by the Maternal and Child Health Services Block Grant Program and the Lead Contamination Control Act of 1988. Grant funding should be appropriated for States to allow its residents to apply for funding in order to replace their portion of the service line. This proven methodology would allow the homeowner to be responsible for acquiring the money for private service line replacement in the form of a grant that does not accumulate interest nor has to be paid back to the funding agency.

comment:
EPA’s Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI)
Public Comment of the National Center for Health Research
(EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036)

The National Center for Health Research is a nonprofit public health think tank in Washington, DC that is dedicated to improving the health and safety of adults and children by using scientific evidence to improve public policies and programs.

We strongly support the numerous improvements in the LCRI, such as the following plans:
1. To eliminate the 10 ppb trigger level, since that level is not supported by the science. The current system built around this trigger is not adequate to protect children or public health.
2. To expand the regulations to include 9 million pipes.
3. To reduce the time frame to 10 years.
4. To base compliance on either the first or fifth liter sample, whichever is higher
5. To require that water systems report all home testing results to the residents within 3 days. Whenever possible, we encourage EPA to urge that testing results be made available even sooner.
6.. To calculate the average annual replacement rate across a rolling three-year period.
7. To require disclosure and offer pipe replacement whenever there is a change in building ownership.

We recommend the following improvements to the proposed rule:

Although EPA’s plan to lower the action level to 10 ppb is an important step in the right direction, we strongly recommend a lower action level of 5 ppb and agree with the AAP that the action level should be 0 ppb.

We urge EPA to require public water systems to be responsible for replacing the entire lead pipe, not only the part that is on public property. Partial pipe replacement should be prohibited except in the rare emergency situation when it is impossible to replace the entire pipe. In addition, we urge EPA to ensure that renters have equitable access to lead service line replacement.

Children’s lead exposures in schools, daycare facilities, and after school care facilities need to be reduced, and that requires greater EPA attention and enforcement to ensure safety. For example, mandatory installation of point-of-use filters on all faucets that are potentially used for drinking makes more sense than merely implementing a testing and monitoring program.

Overall, the regulatory language for reporting lead in water needs to be strengthened and enforced.

In conclusion, it is important to note that lead pipes should not be replaced with pipes that contain lead or other dangerous chemicals. For example, PVC pipes are also very hazardous to human health, because the base material is vinyl chloride, a chemical that has been linked to increased risk of liver, brain, and lung cancers, as well as lymphoma and leukemia.

comment:
As members of the New York League of Conservation Voters, we applaud your Lead and Copper Rule Improvements proposal and encourage you to strengthen and quickly finalize these important safeguards for our families and our drinking water. Lead is a neurotoxin and is especially harmful to children. We know there is no safe level of lead, but still up to 22 million people in this country drink water delivered through lead pipes. The EPA has an incredible opportunity to once and for all get the lead out and protect our families and communities.

The proposal includes a key provision requiring all lead pipes be replaced within 10 years, however, there are exemptions for some cities that could leave our families exposed to lead in drinking water for decades. New York City has nearly 347,000 lead or possible lead service lines. At least 40% of these lead pipes are in Disadvantaged Communities, affecting roughly 738,000 people, a population equivalent to the 19th biggest city in this country, larger than Boston, Washington DC, Baltimore, or Atlanta. Under the EPA's proposal, lead pipe removal in NYC could go on for up to 35 years. Ironically this would create a profound environmental injustice whereby wealthier and whiter communities outside of New York City would be assured cleaner drinking water decades before the city's low-income communities and communities of color. The 35-year timeline would be a disaster for families who live in these communities, and would further delay environmental justice. We urge the EPA to close this loophole and require that every water utility meet the 10-year deadline.

Additionally, we urge the EPA's proposed LCRI to follow examples from states like New York that are leading the way. For instance, data from service line inventories will be more readily available to New Yorkers than the rest of the nation thanks to city and state actions. In NYC, service line data is released publicly every six months. Statewide, water systems serving more than 10,000 people will be required to update their inventories annually starting in 2025. In the area of school drinking water, in 2016 New York was the first state in the nation to create a mandatory testing system. Currently this program is leading the nation with triennial testing and with an action level of 5 ppb.

Finally, since there is no safe level of lead, we urge the EPA to follow the science and get as close to 1 ppb as recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics by reducing the action level from 15 ppb to 5 ppb. Also, paying to replace dangerous lead pipes should not be the responsibility of the homeowner, which would put a disproportionate burden on low-income communities and potentially exclude renters whose landlords refuse to pay. EPA should ensure that the water utilities cover all the costs of full lead service line replacement.

comment: The water utility for the City of Missoula, MT has thousands of galvanized service lines but zero lead service lines have ever been encountered. The customer owns the entirety of the service from the street into the house. Despite the overwhelming weight of evidence that there are no lead services in our system, the LCRI definition of "Galvanized Requiring Replacement" (GRR) is going to force us to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions of dollars, to prove that these customer-owned services do not contain lead. This effort will take away critical financial resources that could be used to solve real problems that exist in our system, including a high rate of leakage and aging infrastructure. We fully understand the importance of removing lead service lines in this country and support the need to inventory all of the services. Our issue is the arbitrary requirement to verify pipe materials in two different locations. We have diligently been working  to gain access to every home in our service area to identify the pipe materials and will have inventoried every water service line within a year or two. Furthermore, we have inventoried hundreds of buried service lines dating back to when the service line inventory was first identified as a potential requirement. We also have original installation records for approximately half of our old service lines. None of those efforts have ever identified a lead service line in our system.   There are no easy or cheap ways to identify the buried portion of each service line. Our curb boxes are too small to use CCTV to identify the piping materials. Vacuum excavating 6-feet down in cobbly soils is an expensive proposition that does not make sense in our system. Statistical methods don't work when the underlying dataset shows zero lead service lines. We ask that a weight of evidence approach be considered when defining GRR services. We are more than happy to validate a sampling of service lines to prove what we already know is the case, that there are no lead services lines. To arbitrarily require us to investigate thousands of potential GRR services that we do not own or control is not the best use of our customer's funds when compared to other system priorities.

Dear Administrator Regan:

Thank you for your leadership around the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) proposal. There’s no safe level of lead exposure, yet communities across the country have navigated the adverse health impacts of lead in drinking water for far too long. The presence of lead pipes is an environmental justice issue and when it’s coupled with other cumulative impacts, such as flooding and air pollution, it’s imperative that we take the necessary steps to right these wrongs, so low-income communities of color aren’t shouldering this burden any longer. The LCRI, as it stands, is a step in the right direction for our nation’s drinking water standards. However, Chicago, the city I’ve called home for 25 years and the city where my loved ones reside, deserves a sense of urgency to tackle its lead pipe issues.

As I review the LCRI proposal, I urge the EPA to reconsider Chicago’s 44.6-55.8 year timeline for replacements. To expedite the replacement process, the EPA should require water systems to fully pay for lead service line replacements. The cost of replacement can be unaffordable, and no resident should have to tolerate a lead pipe delivering water to their home because they can’t afford the cost of replacement. Additionally, no resident should have to wait for a landlord’s permission to replace their lead pipes. As we’ve seen in other cities, the process for replacement is more efficient and equitable when both issues are addressed at the front end.

It’s unconscionable that our kids must continue to consume contaminated drinking water when we have the tools, resources, and expertise at our disposal to take bold, actionable steps to address the issue. We have an opportunity to send a clear message that the health and safety of our most impacted communities are a priority and by pursuing the aforementioned recommendations to strengthen the rule, I have no doubt that generations to come will thrive from an improved quality of life.

I look forward to “getting the lead out” of Chicago’s drinking water with the EPA as a partner in the process. Thank you for your time and consideration!

comment:
As a water resource professional with over 30 years of experience, I have worked in communities dealing with high levels in drinking water. The public health impacts can be irreversible to our children. It is time for a strong and effective lead and copper rule. I am pleased to submit the following comments and recommendations on the proposed LCRI rule. No lead is safe, and the new proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements will significantly benefit lead poisoning prevention efforts and its countless social, health, and economic benefits. Specifically, the updates that require full lead service line replacement, reduce the action level, increase transparency, and require educational material elements are positive improvements.

However, more needs to be done if we are to protect public heath from lead poisoning.
I urge the U.S. EPA to further strengthen this rule by:

-Updating the school and child care facility testing regulations to "require" lead sampling rather than offer it "on request" for all schools and licensed child care facilities. This is essential if we are to protect our most vulnerable population.

-Requiring that local water systems pay for the full service line replacement, because otherwise, the lowest income customers will be disproportionately impacted financially and health-wise.

-Requiring lead pipe replacements to be done using copper, or polypropylene when copper is not feasible, as new pipe materials. If we allow the use of toxic materials, we will create another public health problem.
-Further limiting the exceptions to the 10-year replacement timeline would prolong the exposure to lead in water in the areas with the most lead pipes.

-Strengthening the requirements for filter distribution to obtain compliance of local water systems with multiple Action Level Exceedances in 5 years.
-Require that testing is also done in multi family homes and apartments.
-Provide language for water systems to use that accurately describe action level exceedances. Currently, water systems emphasize that the water leaving the plant does not contain high levels of lead. This is confusing to residents, who aren't familiar with the "compliance testing requirements". Clear and transparent language must be provided to residents so they can make informed decisions to protect their families' health.

Sincerely,
Ms. Ann Baughman

comment:
Dear Mr. Goldberg,

Thank you for your agency's work to update the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper. While I applaud many parts of the proposed rule, there are several weaknesses that need to be addressed as well:

1) Water systems, both public and private, must be required to pay for all lead service line replacements without imposing any additional cost burdens on their customers. Otherwise, end users - many of whom are already struggling to make ends meet - will be left with significant cost burdens, and it will be more difficult to reach the 100% replacement requirement of the new rule.

2) There should be no extensions for water systems to have to remove their lead pipes within the 10-year deadline. A decade is easily adequate, and any extension will cause irreparable harm to countless people and animals.

3) The proposed 10 parts-per-billion (ppb) action level is arbitrary, inadequate, and not at all based on science. The action level should be lowered to any detectable level of lead, as there is no safe level of lead exposure.

4) There must be a universal requirement for the immediate electronic reporting of test results and violations to the EPA and state and local environmental and health agencies, since many lead violations are not reported and thus go unchecked.

5) The rule must require utilities to comprehensively and frequently test for lead from fountains and drinking-water sources in schools and childcare centers, including sources which are not primarily intended for use as drinking-water sources but that may be used as such. Otherwise, parents, children, staff, and visitors will be misled about whether their water is safe, since lead levels vary enormously from tap to tap and from day to day (and as I mentioned in point 3, there is no safe level of lead).

6) Your agency should fully quantify the cost savings from removing lead pipes, as the benefits of doing so extend well beyond lower cardiovascular risks. The cost analysis should particularly examine mental-health and other neurological impacts, as those are most commonly affected by lead pollution.

Please include those additions in the rule before it is finalized so the final rule is as effective and economically beneficial as possible. Thank you.

comment:
I would like to echo my colleague's sentiment on the identification of LSLs:

The EPA has stated that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water. A goal of the LCRI is to
conclusively identify and replace all LSLs in the US by 2037. I applaud this effort and wish to comment on
some of the particulars of these pending regulations.
Accurate identification of lead service lines is a crucial step of this process. I am concerned that
the current approach to identify unknown service lines could cause many service lines to be
misidentified and left in place. Historical records can provide a useful starting place for identification of
service lines; however, many records have been lost or are inconclusive. Millions of service lines are of
unknown material. Excavation is the gold standard for service line identification, but the costs to unearth
non-lead service lines are prohibitively expensive and should be avoided. A two-point visual inspection
of the service line at the meter pit would not identify lead connectors, or LSLs where the meter connects
with a tail of another material [1]. A flushed water sample measuring 2.5 ppb or higher is used in the UK
and France to identify potential LSLs, with high positive identification rates. I propose that a two-step
verification process be required for unknown service line identification, where both a two-point visual
inspection and flushed sample lead is measured. In cases where the lead concentration is above 2.5 ppb
and/or a two-point visual inspection confirms lead, the service line should be labelled as a LSL. In cases
where the water sample is below 2.5 ppb and the two-point visual inspection returns a negative
identification, the line should be considered non-lead. To achieve maximum effectiveness and negate
entry into customers’ homes, the property’s hose bib could be used for water sampling. Additionally, I
propose that a significant proportion of pre 1986 built homes with non-lead lines be tested with this
method to achieve 95 percent confidence in the identification of non-lead service lines through records
alone.
I encourage the EPA to make room for new technologies to aid in water sampling. Portable,
affordable, and easy to use water sensors with sufficient LOD could alleviate some of the burden placed
on labs to complete water testing. New technologies are under development to this end. I would
welcome the approval of New EPA Certified Methods as an Alternate Test Procedures for use in the field
opposed to the requirement for all lead and copper samples to be processed in EPA certified labs. The
new three-day turnaround time will overwhelm these strapped labs. A fast track for verification and
approval of new methods could lower costs while maintaining a high standard for positive identification
of lead in water samples.
-Nick Halverson

A two-point visual inspection is insufficient for the identification of LSLs, and the testing proposed above would both increase our confidence in LSL identification and minimize the cost to do so. As there are no safe levels of lead in drinking water, we should be taking every precaution to ensure the safety of our communities.

Regards,
Arianna LaLonde

comment:
My name is Annika Simpich. I grew up right outside of Washington D.C in Takoma Park, Maryland and I’m currently a junior at the University of Pittsburgh studying political science and law. I am writing to call on the EPA to lower lead concentration from an action level of 15 parts per billion (ppb) to 1 ppb.

In 2004, D.C. experienced the country’s most severe water contamination crisis. A report from D.C. water showing lead contamination over the last 20 years shows that contamination has gone down significantly by 2022. Today, D.C. has the highest clean water rating in the country. Growing up, I never had to worry about the water I drink at school or at home being contaminated by highly toxic chemicals, like lead. When I moved to Pittsburgh, in a state that historically has high rates of water contamination, I had to make a lot of adjustments to how and where I get clean drinking water. My friends who grew up in Pittsburgh and throughout Pennsylvania gave me many recommendations for the best water filters to buy, and which buildings had water filling stations.

Schools across the country are exposed to lead contamination. The state of Pennsylvania received an F grade from Environment America Research and Policy Center for their laws and regulations on the lead contamination of schools’ drinking water. The study was clear: too many kids in Pennsylvania are potentially being exposed to unsafe levels of lead.

Lead contamination is extremely dangerous for our health, and especially for children. Lead exposure causes damage in how children learn, grow and behave. According to Marcie Billings, a pediatrician with the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, lead exposure has shown a rise in “learning difficulties, hyperactivity, and developmental delays.” High levels of lead can also have severe health impacts–including anemia, kidney disease, abnormal brain function, and even death. Due to these health risks, the use of lead gasoline and lead paint has already been federally banned. Let’s get lead out of our water, too.

The best way to lower the lead contamination in school drinking water would be to implement a filter first policy. The filter first policy would require the installation of lead filters on every tap used for drinking water, cooking, or beverage preparation. Fountains with lead fixtures that cannot have filters installed should be removed and replaced with new water stations and filters. Dear Administrator Regan,

The NAACP Virginia State Conference submits the following comments regarding the US Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”). The NAACP Virginia State Conference provides leadership for local branches, youth councils, and college chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in Virginia. The NAACP and its Center for Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring that issues of community engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and frontline communities most impacted, including communities in Virginia.

Our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the proposed LCRI, such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the requirements for water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through lead pipes and a lower action level; but also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which undermine their goals and ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.
We urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not leave Black communities in Virginia behind:

Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a fundamental injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 or more years to fix this issue.

Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted communities will result in mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced. Removal and replacement do not make up major proportions of utility budgets, and utilities should be expected to maximize the use of available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize solving this crisis.

Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many hours there daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead exposure when compared with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing program does not differ from past ineffective programs, and EPA should move towards incentivizing the installation of filters and protecting children.

Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would allow environmental injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline communities have long suffered from disinvestment and lack of resources. Past NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had the strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA of any sociodemographic characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to make significant changes in the lives of millions of people in Virginia and to provide a measure of environmental justice that these families are owed, and we encourage this administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by strengthening the final rule further.

Please note, due to word limit constraints, more details of our concerns and issues in Virginia are listed in the attached letter, 'VirginiaNAACP_Final_Lead and Copper Rule Letter.pdf.

comment:
Proposing stronger regulations to protect people from lead in drinking water is the right step to take, especially because drinking water contamination disproportionately affects low wealth families and communities of color. Ending the nationwide crisis of lead in water should be a priority for this administration and for all Americans.

Requiring removal of all lead service lines in most water systems in ten years is a massive step towards ensuring nobody is living with exposure to lead. Improving sampling requirements and lowering the EPA lead action level are also extremely important to help communities across the nation.

However, we need EPA to ensure the final rule is even stronger or else the goals of the administration will not be met and future generations of children will be exposed to lead from drinking water.

Some crucial improvements would be:
1. Remove the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate that allow some systems to stretch the deadline.
2. Close loopholes allowing water systems to remove some lead service lines from the replacement pool so they need not replace all of them.
3. Mandate water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines and replace them with lines made from sustainably-sourced copper. Work with Congress to provide funding for low income communities. This is a public health issue disproportionately affecting communities of color and low-wealth communities. Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and we must ensure that removal isn't only for the wealthy.
4. Incentivize schools to install filters to ensure that children who spend many hours there daily are no longer at high risk of exposure.

We know lead is a serious problem nationwide, and we cannot allow environmental injustices surrounding it to continue. It is unjust and unfair to force people to endure years, if not decades, more daily lead exposure because they cannot afford to fix their contaminated lead service lines.

Please finalize a strong and equitable rule, so all communities see significant decreases in lead in their drinking water. Ordinary Americans should have safe water supplies. We should not be inadvertently poisoning ourselves with our tap water.

Thank you very much.

Sincerely,
Diane Selvaggio
Gibsonia, PA

comment:
Greetings, everyone. I am Melodie Marsh, a first-year sophomore at the esteemed Howard University, proudly hailing from the resilient city of Flint, Michigan. Today, I stand before you as a representative of the Flint Public Health Youth Academy, speaking passionately on behalf of my community. Having personally witnessed the detrimental impact of lead-contaminated water, as exemplified by the Flint Water Crisis, I emphasize the urgent need for comprehensive revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The Flint Water Crisis, a distressing public health calamity, laid bare the harsh consequences of exposing thousands to hazardous levels of lead. This serves as a stark reminder of the critical necessity for robust regulations to avert similar tragedies in the future. Drawing from this painful chapter, I earnestly implore the EPA to embark on immediate and far-reaching revisions to the LCR.

The current action levels, though designed to prompt action, fall short of adequately safeguarding public health. Furthermore, conflicting standards between the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the EPA regarding the action level create confusion. It is paramount that a unified stance be established, unequivocally asserting that no amount of lead is safe. I urge the EPA to revise the LCR with the overarching goal of achieving zero lead in drinking water.

I advocate for a proactive approach, emphasizing the need for urgent action. Nearly a decade has passed with minimal change in Flint, where residents still grapple with mistrust in their water supply, and essential resources have been diminished. Water distribution sites must be reopened until all lead-lined pipes are replaced, not only in Flint but also in other cities facing a similar crisis. I call for preventative measures, urging the replacement of all lead-lined pipes, supported by federal funding to ensure economic disparities do not hinder compliance.

Moreover, I implore the EPA to involve the community in decision-making processes, valuing the voices of those directly affected by water quality issues. LaTricea Adams, appointed to the White House Environmental Justice Advisory Council at the age of 39, highlights the need for diverse representation. I propose the EPA mandate water systems to establish advisory councils with residents, particularly from vulnerable communities, actively participating in decisions related to water treatment and safety measures.

Transparency and accessibility of water quality data are crucial aspects of a revised LCR. The lack of transparency and delayed action were significant issues in Flint. Mandating water systems to maintain an up-to-date inventory of lead service lines, publicly accessible, and ensuring timely, understandable water quality data, including lead testing results, is imperative.

In conclusion, the Lead and Copper Rule must evolve in reflection of the hard-learned lessons from the Flint water crisis. The proposed revisions are not mere theoretical improvements but arise from the harsh realities faced by my community. It is imperative that the EPA takes decisive action to revise the LCR, prioritizing the health, safety, and well-being of residents to prevent any community from enduring the devastating consequences we have experienced.

comment:
Re: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements
To Whom It May Concern,
We are the Health and Environmental Justice Committee of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) Flint Branch. Our committee includes public health and medical professionals that work to address health and environmental concerns and inequities in the Flint and Genesee County community. Lead exposure during the Flint Water Crisis has negatively impacted our community so we believe in the importance of strong lead regulations that focus on prevention and mitigation via equitable approaches and policies.
We would like to provide feedback on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. In November 2023, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) that provide a critical step to reduce lead in drinking water over the next ten years. We have recommendations that would strengthen these protections to prevent further exposure to lead in environmental justice communities.
Weak lead exposure regulations fail to protect the most vulnerable populations in our community. In Flint, the vulnerable populations include the Black and Brown community, low income households, youth and seniors. Flint is home to approximately 80,000 residents and the median household income is $35,000. There is a large Black and Brown community in Flint, with 56% identifying as African American. Because of sensitive periods of neurodevelopment, it is imperative that kids are protected from the irreversible harms of lead exposure. Here in Flint, 24% of the population is under 18 years and 6.7% of the population is under 5 years. Lead exposure is also particularly harmful for seniors age 65 and up, who make up 13% of the population in Flint. (Census, 2023)
The EPA’s proposal for lead service line replacement is valid but we encourage more robust systems for tracking and stringent regulation of the process across the country. There should be consequences for water systems that do not replace the lead service lines within 10 years. Additionally, it is recommended that lead service line replacement be an opt out procedure in order to be inclusive and equitable in communities where communication is challenging and households residents are not the homeowner. The replacement of lead service lines should be completed and implemented in the most efficient, effective, and equitable way to eliminate exposure to lead and protect public health. There should also be financial prioritization of lead service line replacement in environmental justice communities.

The EPA’s proposal for reducing complexity and improving public health protection was fair, but we encourage this rule to go even further to protect public health. Given that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water, NAACP Flint Branch demands that the federal action level be lowered from 15 ppb, not only to 10 ppb as proposed here, but to 1 ppb to provide the strongest protection possible.
Transparency and communication are vital to maintain and build public trust which is essential for safeguarding public health and eliminating health disparities, especially in environmental justice communities. The EPA should have a public notification process that has diverse communication options including digital (website, social media, radio) and in person (flyers, church announcements, etc) to effectively educate and inform communities. Equitable communication strategies would assist residents in lead exposure notification and alert them to when water-related work is occurring in a timely manner.
Finally, the proposal includes a cost-benefit analysis for making improvements to the Lead and Copper rule. As residents of Flint, we can assure you that there is no dollar amount that could compare to the cost of human life or the irreversible harm caused by lead exposure. In environmental justice communities all across the country, there are people who depend on the government to put forward rules that truly protect our health and well-being no matter the cost.
In closing we appreciate you taking the time to read our comments. Please consider incorporating stricter regulations and stronger protections for drinking water to protect the health of the most vulnerable among us.

comment: The proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) represent a significant step forward in safeguarding public health and addressing concerns related to lead contamination in drinking water. By requiring water systems to replace lead service lines, reducing the lead action level, and strengthening tap sampling procedures, among other changes, the EPA is demonstrating its commitment to improving water quality standards and protecting communities across the country. The removal of the lead trigger level and the simplification of the rule relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) underscore the EPA's efforts to streamline regulatory processes while enhancing public health protection. Moreover, the proposed improvements in corrosion control treatment, public education, requirements for small systems, and sampling in schools and child care facilities signify a comprehensive approach to addressing the challenges posed by lead exposure in drinking water. In ensuring the effectiveness and safety of these measures, regulators should involve agencies like the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), which could provide expertise and guidelines to enhance implementation and protect workers and communities from potential hazards. Importantly, the EPA's focus on mitigating potential disproportionate impacts of lead in underserved communities through initiatives such as lead service line replacement and public education initiatives reflects a commitment to environmental justice and equitable access to clean water resources. Overall, the proposed rule holds promise for significantly improving water quality standards and ensuring the safety and well-being of all individuals who rely on public drinking water systems.

comment:
Dear Ms. Fox and Mr. Regan,

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently proposed improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCRI), which would mandate that all lead service lines be removed within the next 10 years. This proposal, while monumental in making sure communities across this country have access to safe drinking water, still falls short of what is necessary to tackle this public health issue.

I, join GreenLatinos, an active comunidad of over 600 Latino/a/e members and thousands of community leaders living across the U.S., to urge the EPA to consider the following revisions and recommendations to the LCRI, to ensure the administration is doing all it can to guarantee safer drinking water for all.

No amount of lead in water is safe for consumption. While the EPA is proposing to lower the lead action levels from 15 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion, this level is not protective enough. The lead action level dictates when a water system has to inform the public and take action to reduce lead exposure while working to replace the lead pipes. WIth this in mind, the lead action level should be reduced to 5 ppb.

Testing needs to be required in public schools and childcare facilities.

When testing reveals high lead concentrations (above the lead action level), water filters need to be accessible and free to residents. This distribution needs to be paired with community outreach so people have information on the importance of filters and the lead reduction process. This outreach should continue until lead levels are reduced.

Reduce the amount of exceptions to the 10-year lead service line removal requirement. Communities should not have to pay the price of more exposure to lead simply because there are more lead service lines in their water systems.

Water utilities and government agencies must cover the cost of replacing lead pipes without passing the cost on to communities. Additional non-competitive grants and funds should also be made available for water utilities and agencies who do not have enough funding.

Ensuring language justice when informing communities. Make sure public notices and any outreach is done in multiple languages, both on written materials and if resources are shared in person.

Water is a human right. Inequitable access to affordable, clean water continues to impact our community. More stringent lead standards are absolutely critical, along with sufficient funding to ensure that lead pipes are removed and replaced both along main municipal lines as well as lines connecting to residential living areas. Low-income and communities of color already bear a disproportionate burden of environmental degradation; ensuring that costs for replacement of water infrastructure, purification, and water quality monitoring are not passed on to them is essential. Outreach of water quality issues must be accessible in order for our communities to be better informed. We need safe drinking water for all.

Sincerely,
Roy Johnson
FL
